OWNER INTENT 2026-08-01: package Latticefall for a storefront so other people can install and play it. Verbatim: "I anticipate that at some point this game is actually going to be built up and put on the Steam marketplace or another marketplace that I could push it to for other individuals to pull it down and play." This is a spec note and a scouting task, not work to start now — the game is playable but only from the Godot editor, and several things below have to be true before a build is worth shipping to a stranger.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST YET, and each is a real prerequisite rather than a nicety.

(1) NO EXPORT PIPELINE AT ALL. There are no export presets in the repository, no export_presets.cfg, and nothing in tools/ produces a binary. Godot needs export templates matching the exact engine version, and the project targets 4.7 with the GL Compatibility renderer. First task is a headless export producing a Windows executable that launches on a machine with no Godot installed and no repository checkout — and that must be verified on a clean machine or a container, because "it runs on the dev box" proves nothing here; the .godot import cache and the LFS working copy are both present there and neither ships.

(2) THE IMPORT-CACHE ASSUMPTION INVERTS. Everything about this project's local workflow assumes the editor imports assets into .godot/ and that the cache is build output, gitignored, and rebuilt on demand. An exported build has that cache baked into the .pck instead. So the export is the FIRST context in which a missing or stale import is unfixable by the player, and the class_name/global-class-cache trap that makes a scene hang rather than error becomes a shipped hang. Export verification therefore has to include actually playing an anchor from the packaged build, not just confirming the binary starts.

(3) NO LICENCE, AND THE AUDIO POSITION NEEDS RE-READING BEFORE MONEY IS INVOLVED. The repository has no LICENSE file. Decision 038 records that sound effects are synthesised in-repo (fine) and that music is generated under the owner's own subscription — that arrangement needs checking against the generator's terms for COMMERCIAL distribution specifically, which is a different question from personal use and is the owner's call, not an engineering one. Fonts are vendored under addons/ and LFS; their licences need auditing the same way. This is the item most likely to be discovered late and to block a release date.

(4) SAVE COMPATIBILITY BECOMES PERMANENT. progress.json is currently free to change shape because the only player is the owner and the only save is on this machine. The moment a stranger has a save, a schema change is a migration. Decide before release whether saves are versioned and migrated or explicitly disposable, and write it down; tools/save_roundtrip.py already proves round-trip integrity and is the natural place to also prove a migration.

(5) NO CRASH OR TELEMETRY PATH, and no way for a player to report anything. Worth deciding deliberately rather than by omission — this project's whole method is that claims are falsifiable, and shipping to strangers with no signal coming back is the opposite of that.

STOREFRONT SPECIFICS TO SCOUT, not to decide yet. Steam has a one-time app fee per title, requires a bank and tax setup that takes real calendar time to clear, wants store assets at fixed pixel sizes, and expects a build uploaded through steamcmd or the Steamworks SDK — none of which is hard, all of which is lead time. itch.io is the cheap and fast alternative and is the sensible place to put the first public build regardless, because it costs nothing, needs no approval, and exercises the same export pipeline. Recommend scouting itch.io FIRST as the forcing function for (1) and (2), and treating Steam as the second step once a packaged build has survived contact with someone who is not the author.

SEQUENCING NOTE. Do not start this before the Theatre Scale programme's E3 placement work is playable — the board size target moved to 48 squared (decision 073), hand-authoring is dead, and the layout generator (LF-080) is on the critical path. A storefront build of the current 18x15 content would be packaging a game the programme is actively replacing.

PLC-06 needed a build-candidate ordering for the autobuild fallback and PLC-04 does not exist yet, so it carries a minimal deterministic 1-tile fallback scan in scripts/anchor_view.gd instead. That scan is correct and deterministic but it is NOT the candidate lattice PLC-04 is meant to provide, and PLC-06's own task list says to reuse PLC-04's ordering. Revisit when PLC-04 lands: the fallback in anchor_view.gd should be deleted and replaced by whatever PLC-04 exposes, so there is one candidate ordering in the project rather than two that can drift. Low urgency — the fallback only runs for --autoplay and the grading harness never uses it, since the grader sources candidates from _slot_priority() in the rules engines. But two orderings that disagree would be exactly the kind of thing that shows up later as an unexplained difference between what the autobuild does and what the grader says is possible

The lane magnet, as PLC-06's spec described it, ACTIVELY FIGHTS THE PLAYER and was removed after being built and played. It needs a different formulation before anyone attempts it again. THE MECHANISM, measured rather than reasoned about: the free cursor moves along four tile-space diagonals that project to screen up/down/left/right, and each of those four is exactly 45 degrees from any axis-aligned lane tangent. The magnet scored alignment as a dot product against the raw tile-space lane tangent, so on an anchor whose lanes are axis-aligned — which is the common case, and anchor-01 specifically — EVERY direction the player pressed scored as "aligned enough" and the magnet pulled the cursor back toward the lane it was trying to leave. MEASURED: three presses of screen-right from a lane-adjacent start should land at (8.06, 3.94), which is legal; with the magnet enabled it reached (7.57, 3.61), which still returns REASON_LANE_STANDOFF. The player presses away from the lane three times and remains unable to build. A helper that fights the player is worse than no helper, so it was cut rather than tuned — tuning the strength would only have changed how far the fight went. IF IT IS ATTEMPTED AGAIN, the fix is to key the assist off the SCREEN direction the player actually pressed rather than off a raw tile-tangent dot product, so that "I am moving away from the lane" is expressible at all. Note also that snap-on-build already covers most of what the magnet was for: lf_build ring-searches within SNAP_RADIUS 0.6 tiles and lands on the nearest legal position, so a player who aims approximately still gets a clean placement. The magnet was solving a problem that the snap mostly solves already, at the cost of making movement feel wrong, and that trade should be re-justified before the idea comes back

autoloop's spawned session dies instantly with 'Execution error' — whole log is 15 bytes. Plain 'claude -p ... --model sonnet --output-format text' works and returns; the untested difference is --dangerously-skip-permissions. Repro: .cache/autoloop-logs/PLC-07-1785615753.log from 2026-08-01. Until this is understood the loop cannot ship anything: iteration 1 produced an empty branch, iteration 2 refused at preflight.
items.note: WRONG PREMISE, corrected by reading the transcript. The spawned session was not broken: it ran for three minutes, completed /session-start, read the PLC-07 spec and was dispatching a godot-engineer subagent when it took '[Request interrupted by user for tool use]' — the owner's Ctrl-C. 'Execution error' is what 'claude -p' prints when a run is aborted, and the 15-byte log is a session that produced no final text because it never finished. Real defect found instead: Ctrl-C is delivered to the foreground PROCESS GROUP, so it reached the child directly and no parent-side graceful stop could ever have worked. Fixed with start_new_session=True + killpg; reproduced both ways before and after.

items.title: autoloop: if the loop is SIGKILLed, the detached session survives and bills tokens with nobody watching. Its pid is now printed and written to .cache/autoloop-status.json so it can be ended by hand, but reap.py does not know about 'claude' sessions and --status does not check whether that pid is still alive. Teach the reaper about a leased autoloop child.

tools/chronicle.py's esc() is called with quote=False, so a straight double quote in an image caption terminates the alt attribute early and the rest of the caption leaks into the tag as bogus attributes. Found by the chronicler while writing PLC-03's entry, worked around by using curly quotes -- but relying on every author remembering that is exactly the shape of latent bug this project keeps finding in its own instruments. esc() should escape quotes in attribute contexts. Two related generator limits found at the same time and NOT bugs, just undocumented: **bold** in an entry's summary or an image caption renders literally, because both go through esc() rather than render_inline() (the summary becomes meta description, the caption becomes alt); and single-asterisk *emphasis* is unsupported and renders as bare asterisks, which prior published entries contain and are presumably showing live on the site.

MERGING A PULL REQUEST CLOSES NOTHING. PROVEN LIVE 2026-08-01: PR #130 merged with the body line 'Closes PLC-03' and GitHub issue #31 is still OPEN with closedAt=null 37 minutes later. GitHub only acts on 'Closes #<number>' - a spec id in backticks is prose it ignores. MEASURED across 51 merged PRs: 0 contain a resolvable closing keyword; only 3 attempt a 'Closes <SPEC-ID>' phrasing at all; 30 GitHub issues are open; 40 open backlog items are referenced by a PR that already merged (referencing is not fixing - LF-211 was FILED by PR #130 - and the fact that nothing distinguishes the two IS the defect). THREE INDEPENDENT HOLES. (1) No workflow triggers on pull_request closed; gate.yml, parity-shard.yml and parity-windows.yml are open/sync only. (2) tools/issues.py close exists and is good but is a LINE IN A PROMPT (autoloop.py:360) and step 8 of the ship skill, not a mechanism - when the OWNER merges by hand, no code runs at all. (3) There are TWO tracking systems that do not know about each other: backlog.json LF-nnn closed with backlog.py done, and docs/issues/*.md projected to GitHub closed with issues.py close. The ship loop touches the second and never the first. THE FIX, two halves matching the two systems. For docs/issues specs: the PR body carries a resolved 'Closes #N' from the issue id map, so GitHub closes natively and atomically on merge no matter who merges - enforced by a pull_request CI check that fails when a PR names a spec id without a resolvable Closes #N. For backlog LF-nnn: the item is marked done IN THE PR'S OWN COMMIT, since backlog.json is a file in the repo rather than an external system, so merging is what lands it - enforced by a tier-1 gate check. Reported by the owner, who noticed the loop ships a PR and the issue stays in the backlog
items.why: Every merged PR leaves its issue open, so the backlog records what was started and never what is done

items.title: guard.py's engine-cache rule denies READS and even PROSE, not just writes. Hit twice live 2026-08-01. First: a command containing 'du -sh' and 'ls -d' against the cache directory was denied with the LF-075 write/move/delete message, though neither touches a byte. Second and worse: a tools/backlog.py add command was denied because the ISSUE TEXT BEING FILED mentioned the directory by name - the rule matches the literal string anywhere on the command line, including inside a single-quoted argument that is documentation. The rule exists to stop the import cache being rebuilt or moved out from under the owner's running game, and that reason is entirely about MUTATION, so refusing inspection and refusing to let the directory be NAMED are pure false positives. The cost is not the denial itself but that the agent then routes around the guard, which is how a guard stops being trusted. FIX: match on mutating verbs and shell redirections targeting the path, not on the substring. Note the first denial also masked the real question being asked (whether a git worktree gets its own import cache), which is the second-order cost of an over-broad rule - it does not just block, it hides. Verify with guard.py --selftest extended by both of these command shapes as must-allow cases
items.why: A guard that denies harmless reads and its own documentation teaches agents to route around it

items.title: gc.py reported a destruction it could not perform, and counted failures as successes. SUPERSEDES THE ORIGINAL LF-201 TEXT, WHICH WAS WRONG ABOUT THE MECHANISM. Filed as a blocker claiming gc.py --apply would delete a live agent's branch. Reproduced deliberately with a --no-checkout worktree and it does not, for TWO independent reasons: (1) git branch -d '+ lf/repro-201' fails with 'branch not found' because the malformed name was never a real ref, and (2) even parsed correctly git refuses on its own - 'cannot delete branch used by worktree at ...'. What was actually broken. Plain 'git branch --merged' decorates its output with '* ' for the current branch and '+ ' for a branch checked out in ANOTHER WORKTREE. The parser stripped '* ' and not '+ ', so a live agent's branch came back as the literal string '+ lf/thing', matched nothing in the checked-out exclusion set, and printed 'would delete + lf/thing (merged into main)'. The tool was lying about what it would do rather than doing it - which still cost a blocker-priority issue and a session spent believing agent branches were being deleted, and it stayed safe only by accident of a malformed name. THE SECOND, REAL DEFECT, FOUND WHILE FIXING THE FIRST: subprocess.run for both the branch delete and the worktree remove used capture_output with NO return-code check, and incremented the swept counter unconditionally. Every failed removal was silent and still counted toward 'swept N item(s)' - the same class of instrument as the retry loop that committed nothing twelve times without failing. FIXED: --format=%(refname:short) so no decoration ever reaches the delete path; %(worktreepath) from for-each-ref as the authoritative checked-out set rather than parsing worktree list; branches considered BEFORE worktree prune, because pruning de-registers a vanished worktree and that is exactly what disarms git's own refusal; return codes checked, failures printed, exit 1 when any removal failed; and gc.py --selftest asserting both invariants against the repo's real refs rather than a fixture, since the bug was a parsing bug against real git output and a fixture of what someone believes that output looks like is what let it through
items.why: Supersedes LF-201, whose filed mechanism was wrong; the real defect is a lying dry run plus silently-counted failures

items.title: PRC-15 DE-RISKED BY MEASUREMENT: a git worktree DOES get its own fully-populated Godot import cache, so the concern PRC-15 itself calls "the single biggest reason worktrees are not free here" is answered and is not a blocker. MEASURED 2026-08-01 against the live agent worktree at .claude/worktrees/agent-a7712cc56b9f06fe1: 128 MB total, of which 52 MB is its own import cache holding 1378 imported files, against the main tree's 59 MB cache and 1418 files. Two consequences. FIRST, isolation is by construction rather than by configuration: Godot has NO cache-location flag - verified against --help on the real binary, where the only relevant flags are --path <directory> and --import - and --path implies the cache inside that directory, so each worktree is automatically isolated from the tree the owner plays out of. That removes the LF-075 class of risk from worktree agents entirely rather than mitigating it. SECOND, the cost is a one-time import per worktree plus about 128 MB of disk, which is a real cost but a bounded and predictable one, not the open question PRC-15 treats it as. STILL OPEN AND UNMEASURED: the wall-clock of that first import in a fresh worktree, which is the number that decides whether a short-lived agent should get a worktree at all - time it before making isolation the default. ALSO NOTE, and this contradicts PRC-15's spec: the Agent tool's native isolation:"worktree" places worktrees at .claude/worktrees/ INSIDE the main checkout, whereas PRC-15's tasks require them outside it, citing LF-051 (six false nomenclature hits off an agent worktree under .claude/). The gate enumerates with git ls-files rather than rglob now, which is what actually fixed LF-051, so the inside/outside requirement should be re-derived rather than inherited - it may no longer be needed. FOUND WHILE FIXING LF-204: the question was asked once already and the answer was hidden by a guard false positive that denied the read
items.why: PRC-15 is the top process item and its stated blocker turns out to be measurable and bounded

items.title: PLC-07 FOLLOW-UP: remove the tile_slot render asset, which is now drawn by nothing. PLC-07 retired tile_slot from the board -- free placement means legality is a predicate over a continuous position, so there is no set of allowed tiles to paint -- and DECIDED against the alternative the spec named, repurposing it as the buildable-area wash. The reason is the sprite itself: it is a raised bevelled pad with a teal ring and four corner bolts, discrete geometry with real height, and tiled across a region it reads as a field of hardpoints, which reinstates the exact "these are the slots" language PLC-07 exists to remove. A wash has to be a tint, not an object, and it is now a tint over the ground. WHAT IS LEFT is purely mechanical and was deliberately NOT bundled into PLC-07's pull request, because it triggers the art pipeline and a re-import and that is the step which blanks the owner's running game if mishandled (LF-075) -- tangling it with UI work would have made a red sprite atlas check look like a UI regression. THE STEPS, in the order CLAUDE.md fixes: drop tile_slot from render.py's ASSETS dict, drop it from gen_assets.py's PROP_ALLOWLIST (it is a prop, not a data id, which is why asset coverage rather than sprite coverage governs it -- PLC-07's own spec had this backwards and said sprite coverage would fall to 21 of 26; it would not, that check compares enemy and tower ids only), delete the eight PNGs (4 yaws x albedo/glow), re-run pack_atlas.py, re-import, and confirm the sprite atlas check goes green on the new page hash. EXPECT the atlas cell count to fall from 568. ALSO NOTE the C_SLOT constant in anchor_view.gd is now referenced only by the no-atlas fallback path in _draw_board and can go at the same time. Say so before re-importing -- the owner plays out of this same tree
items.why: A render asset nothing draws is a dead atlas cell, and the removal needs an atlas repack the UI work must not be tangled with

items.title: sim/coverage.py's geometric half does not predict its own dynamic tail, and verdict()'s (a)/(b)/(c) label inherits the error. MEASURED across the six LF-185 anchors: anchor-13 (6,0) has 43.9 pct geometric lane_coverage() and 2.5 pct mean uptime; anchor-10 (1,1) has 17.1 pct geometric and 53.7 pct uptime. lane_coverage() is a true statement about the level and should keep its meaning, but it is NOT the predictor the summary treats it as. What actually predicts uptime is PRESENCE-WEIGHTED coverage: the share of live unit-ticks inside range, which needs the lane's kill-progress distribution rather than just its length. On the six anchors half of all live unit-ticks fall in the first 20-25 pct of the lane and the last quarter holds 4-5 pct, so a slot covering lane the enemies never reach alive is idle regardless of distance-to-path or range - which is why sweeping pulse-turret range 3.2 to 7.0 moved p50 28.0->44.5 and left p10 pinned at 0.0. THE WORK: add presence-weighted coverage as a second column beside lane_coverage(), and rewrite verdict()'s '(a) geometry: slots are far from the lane' sentence, which is the wrong diagnosis for the failure it fires on. A scratch implementation exists (200 buckets, profile summed over 20 policies x 3 difficulties) - it was written in the LF-185 pass and is described in that PR

Act 1 and act 2 anchors attrit the wave in the first fifth of the lane; act 3 does not, and that difference IS the residual near-zero tail. MEASURED in live unit-ticks per 5 pct of lane, summed over 20 policies x 3 difficulties: anchor-01 reaches 50 pct cumulative presence by bucket 3 (15 pct of lane) and anchor-13 by bucket 4; anchor-20 not until bucket 9 (45 pct), with 11 pct of presence still in the last quarter. Near-zero emplacement rates track it exactly - act 1 16 pct, act 2 11 pct, act 3 5 pct, after the LF-185 re-siting pass. CONSEQUENCE: slot re-siting can only move guns INTO the live zone, it cannot lengthen the live zone, so the tail migrates rather than vanishing (post-LF-185, anchor-11 (2,8) is 45/51 near-zero and anchor-13 (10,4) is 34/57 - slots that were fine before). Chasing near-zero to zero converges on every slot stacked at the lane entrance, which is fitting to the metric and is exactly what decision 067 rejected. THE LEVER for the rest is enemy hp/speed/spawn pressure in the act 1-2 wave tables, not slot geometry. This is BAL-04 territory and it WILL move the grades, so it must be graded as a balance pass rather than bolted onto a siting change. Note LF-187 already says decision 074's range numbers must be re-derived at 48x48 anyway

data/schema/anchor.schema.json types slot coordinates as integer, which contradicts PLC-01's continuous positions and contradicts several briefs. VERIFIED in the LF-185 pass: sim/content.py loads slot coordinates as float64 and Sim._placement_reason() accepts any float, so the engines are continuous end to end - but a fractional slot in an anchor file is a SCHEMA ERROR today and validate_data.py will reject it. This mattered concretely: the LF-185 re-siting was told slots may be fractional, searched integer positions only after discovering the schema, and may have left better sub-tile positions unreachable. THE WORK is one of two, and it is a real choice rather than a typo fix: either widen the schema to 'number' so authored slots can use the continuous space the rules already model, or stop repeating the 'slots may be continuous floats now' claim in briefs and docs and make integer-only explicit. Prefer widening - PLC-04's candidate lattice will want sub-tile positions and the rules already accept them

anchor-02 brutal lost two distinct winning builds (6 -> 4) in the LF-185 re-siting pass. Recorded so it is not later discovered as an unexplained narrowing. Still clean - sim/run.py reports ok=True, death wave unchanged at 2, and four distinct winning builds is well above the single-solution floor - and it is the ONLY cell of 18 (six anchors x three difficulties) that narrowed; distinct viable builds went UP on anchor-10, 11, 12, 13 and on anchor-08 standard. The likely mechanism is that concentrating slots into the high-presence early stretch of the lane makes a few strong sitings dominate, which removes weaker but previously-viable build orders. If anchor-02 brutal narrows further in any subsequent pass, this is the entry to start from. Before/after grade JSON was produced in the LF-185 pass

sim/coverage.py --selftest was RED on main and nothing noticed, because NO GATE TIER RUNS IT. Found during the LF-217 pass and fixed there, but the gap is the real item. MECHANISM: the selftest's far-slot probe built at (500,500) to prove a slot with zero coverage measures zero; PLC-02's _placement_reason() then began answering out_of_bounds for that position, so the scheduled build stopped landing and the selftest failed with 'the scheduled build never landed' - a message about the harness, not about coverage. Proved against git show HEAD:sim/coverage.py run in isolation: 'HEAD placed slots: []'. Fixed in LF-217 by widening the in-memory probe anchor to 40x40 and moving the probe to (30,30); data/ untouched. WHY IT MATTERS: this selftest is the ONLY runtime proof that InstrumentedSim cannot move an Outcome - it runs the same (anchor, policy, difficulty) through both Sim and InstrumentedSim and asserts the Outcomes are field-for-field identical. Without it in the gate, a rules change in an unrelated workstream can silently invalidate every coverage measurement the project takes, and did, for at least two merges with nothing red anywhere. THE WORK: put it in a tier. It is ~2m43s in full, which is too expensive for tier 2 (already over its 28000ms budget, LF-178) - so either tier 3/4, or add a cheap variant that runs only the outcome-parity leg on a single anchor and put THAT in tier 2. Prefer the cheap variant plus the full run at tier 4

PLC-04's candidate lattice ENLARGES LF-053/LF-095 rather than solving it, and PLC-04 must not be read as a fix for them. Every Policy is a total preference order and _try_build fills greedily from the top, so a graded build is all-of-one-thing. With 12 authored slots that produced 'twelve arc nodes'; with the ~366-763 legal lattice candidates per anchor at half-tile pitch it produces 'as many as _effective_cap() and the money allow'. MEASURED during the PLC-04 pass. The count has not actually moved yet because _effective_cap() still falls back to len(slots) - the day that fallback goes, it will. BAL-02's capped-core policies are the fix. Recorded here because PLC-04's own spec asks for the note and because a bigger candidate set makes a monoculture build look more deliberate than it is

Re-sweep anchor-01, anchor-04, anchor-09 and anchor-11 against PLC-04's lattice grader. Decision 081 adopted round-robin x per-lane maximin as the lattice ordering on BOARD QUALITY grounds and explicitly WITHDREW PLC-04's acceptance criterion 6 ('every anchor still grades ok') as an invalid selector - board quality and grade count were measured anti-correlated across five orderings, with the best-scoring candidate (minimum separation 2.5, 23/24) producing boards nobody would defend and the adopted one (20/24) producing the only board indistinguishable from a hand-authored layout. THE FOUR FAILURES ARE A RE-BALANCE, NOT AN ORDERING PROBLEM: anchor-01 brutal unwinnable, anchor-04 brutal single-solution, anchor-09 brutal single-solution, anchor-11 hard single-solution plus brutal unwinnable. Three of the four are brutal-only and all four boards are well shaped. The cause is that these anchors' capacities, funds and wave tables were swept against a grader confined to their authored slots, so a grader that places well finds those tiers genuinely thin at the top difficulty. THE WORK: tools/sweep.py per anchor, then reconcile the capacity ladder to a monotone envelope BY HAND and re-run tools/say_capacity.py - PLC-04's spec warns that a sweep proves nothing outside its grid and tunes one anchor blind to the others. This is BAL-04 territory and it should be graded as a balance pass

Nothing in the gate asserts that every anchor grades ok. DISCOVERED during PLC-04: the 'sim determinism' check returned FAIL on sim/run.py's exit code BEFORE comparing its two runs, and run.py --json exits 1 whenever an anchor is not clean - so the conflation was accidentally serving as an all-anchors-clean assertion, under the wrong name, with an empty message (run.py writes its verdict to stdout, and the check reported stderr). Decision 081's re-siting of that check to compare outputs first is correct and shipped with PLC-04, but it removes the accidental safety net. THE WORK: add a real 'anchor grades' check that runs sim/run.py over all 24 and fails on any anchor not ok, with the failing anchors and their problem strings in the message. DO NOT ADD IT UNTIL LF-223 LANDS - anchor-01, 04, 09 and 11 are knowingly below ok right now as a consequence of the lattice grader placing better than the sweep those anchors were tuned against, and a check that is red on arrival gets disabled rather than fixed. Cost: a full sim/run.py --jobs 8 is ~60 s, so tier 3 or 4, not tier 2 (already over budget, LF-178)
